\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:ta-please}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell an emphatic \ta{தயவுசெய்து} from the everyday courtesy that lives in the -\ta{உங்கள்} verb ending, and I can write \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்} from hearing.}

Ask for something twice — \ta{தயவுசெய்து} when the request needs weight, plain \ta{உட்காருங்கள்} when it does not — read the join in \ta{செய்து}, and write \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்} from hearing.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tayavu seytu]{\ta{தயவுசெய்து} (tayavu seytu) — please (do the kindness)}

\label{lesson:TA-C08-tayavuseytu}



\begin{quote}
Across a whole band of Asia, the word for \emph{please} is really the word \textbf{compassion}, dressed as a small request. Tamil says it most literally of all: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{do} the kindness.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The phrase}
\textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}} = \textbf{please}, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{do the kindness / grace}.\textquotedblright{} It is two pieces snapped together:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{தயவு}} (\emph{tayavu}) = \textbf{kindness, compassion, grace} — from Sanskrit \textbf{daya} \textquotedblleft{}compassion.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ta{செய்து}} (\emph{seytu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done},\textquotedblright{} from the verb \textbf{\ta{செய்}} (\emph{sey}) \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{tayavu seytu} is an invitation: \emph{do me the kindness (of…)}. You place it in front of a request the way English puts \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} in front of one.

This is the same instinct as \textbf{Arabic} \emph{min faḍlik} (\textquotedblleft{}from your \textbf{grace}\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{Hindi} \emph{kṛpayā} (from \emph{kṛpā}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{compassion}\textquotedblright{}). Naming the kindness you hope for is one of the great strategies of politeness — different from French's \textquotedblleft{}if it \textbf{pleases} you,\textquotedblright{} and from Latin/German's \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{ask}.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
All four Dravidian cousins build \emph{please} the very same way — \textbf{daya} plus a light verb \textquotedblleft{}do / place / become\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}} \emph{tayavu \textbf{sey}tu} — kindness \textbf{+ do}
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು}} \emph{daya\textbf{viṭṭu}} — compassion \textbf{+ having placed}
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{daya\textbf{cēsi}} — compassion \textbf{+ having done}
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} \emph{daya\textbf{vāyi}} — compassion \textbf{+ as / having become}
\end{itemize}

One idea, four scripts. Learn one and you can almost read the others.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tayavu\textquotedblright{} — the kindness — then \textquotedblleft{}seytu,\textquotedblright{} having done
  \item the whole phrase — \textquotedblleft{}tayavu seytu\textquotedblright{} = please, do the kindness
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Tamil phrase for please? (\textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}} \emph{tayavu seytu}.) What do its two pieces mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Kindness}\textquotedblright{} \emph{tayavu} + \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done}\textquotedblright{} \emph{seytu} — \emph{do the kindness}.) Which languages ask the same way? (\textbf{Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam} with \emph{daya}, and further off \textbf{Arabic} \emph{faḍl} and \textbf{Hindi} \emph{kṛpā}.) Next: decide when the standalone phrase is natural and when the verb carries the courtesy.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[solluṅgaḷ]{Solluṅgaḷ — please tell me}

\label{lesson:TA-C08-sollungal}



\begin{quote}
You know \emph{tayavu seytu}, the weightier “do me the kindness.” Now learn one ordinary respectful request by ear before meeting its written shape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: one useful request}
\emph{\textbf{Solluṅgaḷ}} means \textbf{please tell me}. The ending \emph{-uṅgaḷ} makes the request respectful. For now, keep the whole expression together: one sound, one useful meaning.

Say it in three easy pulses: \emph{sol · luṅ · gaḷ}. Then say it smoothly once: \emph{solluṅgaḷ}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{solluṅgaḷ} $\to$ YOU CHOOSE: “please tell me”
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sol · luṅ · gaḷ} — then \emph{solluṅgaḷ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you respectfully ask someone to tell you? (\emph{\textbf{Solluṅgaḷ.}}) Keep that sound and meaning in mind. Next you will uncover just one new written sign inside this already-familiar request.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[so]{\ta{சொ} — one new sign in a familiar request}

\label{lesson:TA-W08-short-o-observe}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{solluṅgaḷ}: \textbf{please tell me}. Its first sound is \emph{so}. You already know the sound and meaning; today only its written vowel sign is new.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ொ}}
The consonant \textbf{\ta{ச}} begins with \emph{ca}. Add the short-\emph{o} sign \textbf{\ta{ொ}}, and it reads \emph{so}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ச} + \ta{ொ} $\to$ \ta{சொ}}
\end{quote}

The short-\emph{o} sign reaches around its consonant. Part appears on the left and part on the right, but together they are one vowel sign. Read the whole joined shape as one syllable: \textbf{\ta{சொ}}, \emph{so}.

Do not invent a stroke order from the printed font. Follow the model as one shape today.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\ta{சொ}} once with the model visible. Say \emph{so} as your finger reaches the vowel sign. Then point to the first syllable in \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} and say the whole familiar request, \emph{solluṅgaḷ}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{சொ}}. (\emph{\textbf{So.}}) What does the whole spoken request \emph{solluṅgaḷ} mean? (\textbf{Please tell me.}) One new sign is enough for today.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[solluṅgaḷ]{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்} — one visible copy}

\label{lesson:TA-W08-sollungal-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to \textbf{\ta{சொ}} at the start of \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}}. Read \emph{so}, then say the whole request: \emph{solluṅgaḷ}, \textbf{please tell me}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} once beneath its visible model. Pause after \textbf{\ta{சொ}} and check that the short-\emph{o} sign reaches around \textbf{\ta{ச}}. Look back after every piece if needed. Say the request once when you finish.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Point to the short-\emph{o} syllable in \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}}. (\textbf{\ta{சொ}}.) What does the word ask? (\textbf{Please tell me.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[solluṅgaḷ]{Solluṅgaḷ — hide, then write}

\label{lesson:TA-W08-sollungal-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Study \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} for five seconds. Point to \textbf{\ta{சொ}}, say \emph{solluṅgaḷ}, then cover the model.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Write \textbf{\ta{சொ}} while the model is hidden. If that feels secure, continue and write the whole request. Peek once if needed, cover it again, and finish. Then uncover the model and repair only the short-\emph{o} syllable.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What changed from the previous step? (\textbf{The model was hidden before writing.}) Say what your word means. (\textbf{Please tell me.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[solluṅgaḷ]{One heard request — write it}

\label{lesson:TA-W08-sollungal-dictation}



\begin{quote}
Cover every Tamil model. You will hear the same useful request you have already said, traced, copied, and retrieved.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — dictation}
{[}YOU HEAR: \emph{solluṅgaḷ} — \textbf{please tell me}{]}

Write the request from sound alone. Then uncover \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}}. Check \textbf{\ta{சொ}} first: the short-\emph{o} sign should reach around \textbf{\ta{ச}}. Repair one place if needed; do not rewrite the whole word.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Without looking, write only the opening syllable of \emph{solluṅgaḷ}. (\textbf{\ta{சொ}}.) You are ready to compare this ordinary respectful request with the weightier \emph{tayavu seytu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tayavu seytu / uṅgaḷ]{\ta{தயவுசெய்து} or -\ta{உங்கள்}? — politeness in phrase or verb}

\label{lesson:TA-C08-please-register}



\begin{quote}
Tamil has a phrase meaning \textquotedblleft{}do the kindness,\textquotedblright{} but everyday courtesy often sits somewhere English speakers do not expect: inside the verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
A standalone \textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}} is more emphatic and formal than English \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} Ordinary polite commands use respectful \textbf{-\ta{உங்கள்}} (\emph{-uṅgaḷ}):

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{உட்காருங்கள்}} \emph{uṭkāruṅgaḷ} — please sit
  \item \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} \emph{solluṅgaḷ} — please tell me — the request you can now say, read, and write from hearing
\end{itemize}

Use \emph{tayavu seytu} to mark \textquotedblleft{}please, do me the kindness\textquotedblright{} warmly or formally. Let the verb ending carry routine courtesy.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: Read the join in \ta{செய்து}}
\textbf{\ta{செ}} is \emph{ca} with the \textbf{\ta{ெ}} sign for \emph{e}. \textbf{\ta{ய்}} is \emph{ya} shut off by puḷḷi, a bare \emph{y}, before \textbf{\ta{து}} \emph{tu}. The same dot that built numbers now makes the consonant seam in \emph{seytu} visible.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Choose:} emphatic request $\to$ \textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}}
  \item \emph{Choose:} ordinary \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{உட்காருங்கள்}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} — and point to \textbf{\ta{சொ}}, the short-\emph{o} syllable
  \item \emph{Break apart:} \ta{செ} + \ta{ய்} + \ta{து} $\to$ \ta{செய்து}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What carries everyday \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}? (The respectful verb ending \emph{\textbf{-uṅgaḷ}}.) When is \emph{tayavu seytu} especially useful? (A \textbf{markedly polite or emphatic} request.) What silences \emph{y} in \textbf{\ta{ய்}}? (The \textbf{puḷḷi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na]{\ta{ந} — the third n, and the only one built from uprights}

\label{lesson:TA-S04-na}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the sound of \textbf{\ta{ன}}.

One letter this time. Just one.

The third n, and the one that finally looks different: no spiral loop at all. \ta{ந} is built from a top bar and two uprights, with a right stroke that curls below the baseline. If you can see that it has no loop, you can already tell it from the other two.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ந}}
\textbf{\ta{ந}} — \emph{na}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a straight top bar
  \item a vertical on the left
  \item a second vertical in the middle
  \item a right stroke that curls below the baseline and sweeps left into a descender
\end{itemize}

\ta{நன்றி} — \emph{thank you} — opens with it, and so does \ta{நான்}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{ந}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the lower-left tail and sweep around the low bowl to its upper junction
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, climb to the top and carry left along the bar to the first descent
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, draw the first upright straight down — then lift once
  \item \textbf{4.} set the pen at the bottom of the adjacent middle upright and rise to the top
  \item \textbf{5.} without lifting again, carry the top bar to the right edge — then lift a second time
  \item \textbf{6.} set the pen at the upper right curve, descend around it and sweep left into the below-baseline tail — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order, not a national standard — Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 12, \ta{ந} (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 195.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{ந} once, slowly, following the steps above
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}na\textquotedblright{} as you finish it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} it twice more, without looking back at the steps
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three n's has no spiral loop? (\textbf{\ta{ந}}.) How many pen lifts does it take? (\textbf{Two}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vaṇakkam]{\ta{வணக்கம்} — the first whole written word}

\label{lesson:TA-W03-write-vanakkam}



\begin{quote}
You know the four letter bodies and the vowel-killing dot. Assemble them left to right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: Build the word}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{வ}} & \emph{va} & Lesson 1 \\
\textbf{\ta{ண}} & \emph{ṇa} & Lesson 2 \\
\textbf{\ta{க்}} & \emph{k} — \ta{க} with the dot & last lesson \\
\textbf{\ta{க}} & \emph{ka} & Lesson 1 \\
\textbf{\ta{ம்}} & \emph{m} — \ta{ம} with the dot & this lesson \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{வ} · \ta{ண} · \ta{க்} · \ta{க} · \ta{ம்} $\to$ \ta{வணக்கம்}}
\end{quote}

Hear two details. \textbf{\ta{க்க}} is a \textbf{doubled} consonant: hold it, \emph{vaṇak-kam}, not \emph{vaṇakam}. Tamil distinguishes single from double consonants. Final \textbf{\ta{ம்}} is a bare \emph{m}, so the word closes instead of trailing into \emph{ma}.

That is the first word of this book, written by hand.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{க்} — \ta{க} with the dot
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{க்க} — two full letters, dot intact
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} — five pieces, left to right
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}vaṇa\textbf{k-k}am\textquotedblright{} — hold the middle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}. What is special about \textbf{\ta{க்க}}? (It is \textbf{doubled} and held.) Why does the word end in \emph{m}, not \emph{ma}? (Final \textbf{\ta{ம்}} carries a \textbf{puḷḷi}.) Next: the formal way to say \emph{please forgive me}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\ta{எ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TA-S112-letter-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ta{◌ோ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{எ}}
\textbf{\ta{எ}} — \emph{e}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape the vowel \emph{e} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ta{எ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{என்}} \emph{eṉ} — my
  \item \textbf{\ta{என்} \ta{பெயர்} …} \emph{eṉ peyar …} — my name is… (with no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ta{என்ன}} \emph{eṉṉa} — what
  \item \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}} \emph{eppaḍi} — how
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{எ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ta{எ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ta{எ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ta{என்}  ·  \ta{வணக்கம்}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{எ} three times, saying \emph{e} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ta{எ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{எ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{e}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
